title: A hymn in Bihagra
hook: inside the Bihagra ballad, a salok headed with Mardana's name talks about wine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bihagra, where Guru Ram Das calls his soul my dear life, and your line was night longing. A new week begins, still at night.

A wine jar, a cup, and someone drinking far too much. Not the picture one might expect inside a holy book's night raga. But there it is, in the ballad of Bihagra in the Guru Granth Sahib. Between the ballad's stanzas sit short verses called saloks, and some of them carry a heading with a name: Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion, the rabab player who traveled with him.
screen: `A WINE JAR AND A CUP.` → `A SALOK HEADED MARDANA.` → `INSIDE THE NIGHT BALLAD.`

segments.voice: The ballad is the Var of Bihagra, with stanzas by Guru Ram Das and saloks set between them. One salok, headed Mardana, paints the scene, in plain English. This dark age is the wine jar. Desire is the wine. The mind is the one drinking. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and pride is the one pouring. Anyone who's watched someone lose a night to drinking knows the picture: the cup keeps getting filled, and the drinker keeps reaching. The salok says the mind does the same with desire. Then it turns the picture around. Make the body the still, it says, and from it draw a different drink, one that runs like nectar. In the company of the holy, the cup becomes loving attention, filled with that nectar, and drinking it cuts the faults away. The night raga fits: the longing that might pour itself into the wrong cup is turned toward God. Now, who wrote it? The heading names Mardana along with the mark the Granth uses for Guru Nanak, and Sikh readers take that in more than one way. Some Sikh scholars read these saloks as Guru Nanak's own words, spoken to Mardana or about him. Others read the heading as giving the words to Mardana himself. The Granth doesn't stop to settle it, and neither does this lesson. Either way, a companion's name stands on the page beside the Guru's, in a ballad sung at night. The longing doesn't vanish. It finds its proper cup.
screen: `THE DARK AGE IS THE WINE JAR.` · `DESIRE THE WINE, THE MIND THE DRINKER.` · `A DIFFERENT CUP: LOVING ATTENTION.` · `MARDANA'S NAME ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `LONGING AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you reached for late at night, scrolling, snacking, one more episode, one more glass, and just see the reach, without judgment. Then ask what the reach was really for, rest, company, comfort, quiet, and hold that real wish for a moment. If you pray, offer it with Waheguru; if you don't, simply name the wish to yourself.

A hymn in Bihagra. A salok in the Bihagra ballad, headed with Mardana's name, where desire is the wine and the mind the drinker, until loving attention becomes the cup and nectar the drink. Today's word.
Your line: longing at night. Desire was the wine; loving attention becomes the cup. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Why is there a wine jar in a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib?
options: A picture: desire is the wine and the mind the drinker, until loving attention is the cup.
It's a riddle: each object in it stands for one of the ragas named in the Granth.
It's a rule for gurdwara kitchens, listing which drinks may and may not be served there.
